title: AI-enabled management is turning surveillance, work intensity, autonomy and data use into psychosocial work conditions requiring integrated rights and health governance
source_unit: International Labour Organization, AI systems @ work: a changing psychosocial work environment, ILO Working Paper 170
geography: Global policy and occupational-safety analysis of AI and digitalization across employment settings

observations.period: 2026 report; AI across the employment relationship

denominator.unit: global employment-cycle and workplace policy synthesis

employment_cycle_scope.value: AI is increasingly used across recruitment, work organization, monitoring and performance management
employment_cycle_scope.unit: reported scope of workplace AI use

psychosocial_environment.value: AI changes the mental and social conditions under which work is performed, not only the technical content of tasks

risk_governance_gap.value: existing occupational-safety and health approaches may not yet fully address AI-associated psychosocial risks

observations.method: ILO working-paper synthesis of AI workplace uses, occupational safety and health concepts, psychosocial risk research and regulatory developments.
observations.uncertainty: The paper is a policy and evidence review, not a prevalence estimate or causal evaluation of any single AI system; effects depend on design, deployment, sector, worker participation and institutional safeguards.
observations.subgroup: Workers, job applicants, managers, platform workers, employees subject to monitoring or automated evaluation, and occupational-safety and health institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI can improve safety, support decision-making and reduce hazardous exposure when workers have transparency, participation, human support and meaningful avenues for correction.

observations.period: 2026 report; augmented psychosocial risks from AI-based systems

denominator.unit: AI-associated psychosocial-risk taxonomy and evidence review

surveillance.value: intensive or intrusive monitoring can create psychosocial risk

work_intensification.value: AI-enabled measurement and optimization can increase work pressure and intensify the pace or volume of work

autonomy_and_dignity.value: algorithmic direction and evaluation can reduce job autonomy and affect dignity at work

privacy_data_concern.value: excessive data collection and limited transparency can create additional psychosocial and rights risks

observations.method: ILO review of psychosocial factors at work and emerging or augmented risks associated with AI-based systems, including surveillance, autonomy and data transparency.
observations.uncertainty: These are risk pathways identified in the literature and policy analysis; the paper does not assign a common probability, severity score or population prevalence to each risk.
observations.subgroup: Workers in digitally monitored settings, platform and logistics workers, employees managed through data-driven systems, and workers with limited bargaining or appeal power.
observations.counterinterpretation: Monitoring may identify hazards or support fairer workload management when its purpose is limited, data use is transparent, workers can contest decisions and human judgment remains accountable.

observations.period: 2026 report; integrated policy response to AI-related psychosocial risks

denominator.unit: cross-domain labour, equality, occupational-health and data-governance policy synthesis

integrated_policy.value: effective response requires labour and employment law, equality and non-discrimination, occupational safety and health, and privacy and data protection to work together

high_risk_regulation.value: employment uses of AI are increasingly treated as high-risk in developing general AI regulatory frameworks

new_osh_rights.value: the paper identifies emerging needs for rights related to transparency, participation, data use, human oversight and protection from psychosocial harm

observations.method: ILO analysis of regulatory frameworks and national policy responses addressing AI-associated psychosocial risks and occupational safety and health.
observations.uncertainty: The report maps policy directions and gaps rather than evaluating enforcement, employer compliance, worker awareness or outcomes in specific jurisdictions.
observations.subgroup: Workers, employers, regulators, unions, equality bodies, occupational-health professionals, data-protection authorities and AI system providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Layering multiple legal regimes can create fragmented responsibility; integrated governance will matter only if rights are understandable, enforceable, resourced and usable by workers.

boundary: This record adds an AI-to-psychosocial-work route: surveillance, work intensification, reduced autonomy, dignity, data use and transparency are treated as work conditions and governance issues. It is an ILO working-paper synthesis, not worker-level mental-health data, a workplace audit, a prevalence estimate, a legal determination or a causal evaluation of AI deployment.
